description: Reading the H-R diagram, tracing stellar evolution paths, and using Cepheid variables as distance indicators.
content_html:
A Map of the Stars

In the early twentieth century, Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell independently discovered that stars are not randomly scattered in terms of their temperature and luminosity — they fall into distinct groups. The Hertzsprung-Russell diagram (H-R diagram) plots luminosity against surface temperature and is one of the most powerful tools in astronomy. Understanding how to read and sketch it is essential.

Key Fact

The H-R diagram has two unusual axis conventions: the y-axis runs from low luminosity at the bottom to high luminosity at the top; the x-axis runs from high temperature on the left to low temperature on the right (opposite to most graphs). The Sun sits near the middle of the main sequence at spectral type G, with luminosity 1 solar luminosity.

Regions of the H-R Diagram

Most stars (about 90%) fall along a diagonal band from the upper-left to the lower-right, called the main sequence. The Sun sits in the middle of the main sequence. Stars spend the bulk of their lives here, steadily fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores. Upper-left main-sequence stars are hot, blue, and far more luminous than the Sun; lower-right stars are cool, red, and dim.

Other regions house stars at later evolutionary stages:

  • Red giants — upper-right of the diagram: cool (red) but very luminous because they are enormously large. A Sun-like star expands into this region after leaving the main sequence.
  • Supergiants — above the red giants, extending across the top of the diagram: these are the most luminous stars, both red supergiants (cool, enormous) and blue supergiants (hot, extremely luminous).
  • White dwarfs — lower-left: hot but very dim, because they are small — roughly Earth-sized. Despite their high surface temperature, their tiny surface area means they radiate little total energy.

Luminosity depends on both temperature and surface area. A white dwarf’s surface temperature can be 20,000 K or more (hotter than the Sun), but its radius is only about 1% of the Sun’s — roughly the size of Earth. Total energy output (luminosity) scales as the surface area times the temperature to the fourth power. Despite high temperature, the tiny area makes white dwarfs very dim. This is why they plot in the lower-left of the H-R diagram: hot, but low luminosity. This is also why the H-R diagram position of a star does NOT represent its location in space — it plots properties, not position.

Stellar Evolution Tracks on the H-R Diagram

A star’s position on the H-R diagram changes as it evolves. The diagram does not show stars moving in space; it shows their changing temperature and luminosity over millions or billions of years. A Sun-like star spends about 10 billion years on the main sequence. As its core hydrogen is exhausted, it begins to expand: its outer layers cool (moving rightward) while luminosity increases (moving upward), eventually becoming a red giant. The star then sheds its outer layers as a planetary nebula and the hot remnant core cools slowly as a white dwarf, moving leftward then downward in the H-R diagram.

High-mass stars follow a different track. They are born as blue supergiants (upper-left), then expand rapidly into red supergiants (upper-right), and end in a supernova explosion. The remnant becomes a neutron star or black hole, which are too small and dim to appear on the conventional H-R diagram.

Star Clusters and the H-R Diagram

All stars in an open cluster formed at the same time from the same gas cloud, so they all began at the same point on the main sequence. Over time, the most massive (upper-left) stars evolve off the main sequence first. By plotting a cluster’s H-R diagram, astronomers can estimate its age from the “main-sequence turn-off point” — the luminosity level at which stars are just starting to leave. Older clusters have lower turn-off points. Globular clusters, found in the galactic halo, are ancient (often 10-13 Gyr old) and have very low turn-off points.

Key Fact

More massive main-sequence stars are far more luminous and burn their hydrogen fuel much faster despite having more of it. A star 10 times the Sun’s mass may last only tens of millions of years on the main sequence; the Sun will last about 10 billion years; a very low-mass red dwarf may last hundreds of billions of years.

Variable Stars

Some stars change in brightness regularly. Variable stars can be intrinsic (the star itself changes) or extrinsic (something blocks the light). On a light curve — a graph of brightness (or magnitude) against time — variable stars show repeated cycles of brightening and dimming.

Cepheid variables are yellow supergiants that pulsate with periods of 1-70 days. Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered in 1908 that the pulsation period is directly related to the star’s luminosity (the period-luminosity relation): longer period = higher luminosity. This makes Cepheids exceptional standard candles — by measuring the period, astronomers know the true luminosity, and combining this with the apparent brightness gives the distance via the distance modulus. Cepheids were used by Edwin Hubble to measure the distance to the Andromeda Galaxy, proving it lies far beyond the Milky Way.

Eclipsing binaries are two stars orbiting each other in a plane nearly edge-on to us. When one star passes in front of the other, it blocks some light — producing a dip in the light curve. Two dips per orbit occur: a deeper one when the brighter star is eclipsed, and a shallower one when the dimmer star is eclipsed. The orbital period and relative sizes and temperatures of both stars can be extracted from the light curve shape.

Novae occur in binary systems where a white dwarf accretes hydrogen from a companion star. Accumulated hydrogen eventually undergoes runaway nuclear fusion on the white dwarf’s surface, producing a sudden dramatic brightening (the nova) before fading over weeks or months. A nova does not destroy the white dwarf; it may recur.
exam_tip_html: The most common H-R diagram mistake is plotting temperature increasing left to right — the opposite of the correct convention. Always mark the high-temperature end on the LEFT and state this explicitly in exam answers. The H-R diagram does not represent physical positions in space: a star’s H-R position shows its temperature and luminosity at that moment in its life. For Cepheid variable questions, the key chain is: measure period → read luminosity from period-luminosity graph → compare with apparent brightness → calculate distance modulus → get distance. Eclipsing binary light curves always show two dips of different depths per orbital period.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The H-R diagram plots luminosity (y-axis, high at top) against temperature (x-axis, high on LEFT). Most stars lie on the main sequence; red giants are upper-right; white dwarfs are lower-left.
  • Stars evolve across the H-R diagram — the diagram shows changing properties over time, not physical motion. Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs; high-mass stars end as supernovae, then neutron stars or black holes.
  • Cepheid variables have a period-luminosity relation that makes them distance indicators (standard candles). Eclipsing binaries show two dips per orbit; their light curves reveal orbital periods and stellar properties.

practice_questions.text:
On a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, in which direction does temperature increase along the x-axis?
A) Left to right
B) Right to left
C) Bottom to top
D) Top to bottom
State the region of the H-R diagram where white dwarfs are found, and give one reason why they plot there despite having high surface temperatures.
practice_questions.marks: White dwarfs are found in the lower-left of the H-R diagram [1]. Despite high surface temperature, they are very small (roughly Earth-sized), so their total surface area and therefore luminosity is very low [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain how astronomers use the main-sequence turn-off point on an H-R diagram of a star cluster to estimate the cluster's age.
practice_questions.marks: All stars in a cluster formed at the same time [1]. The most massive (brightest) stars leave the main sequence first because they burn hydrogen faster [1]. The luminosity level at which stars are currently leaving the main sequence (the turn-off point) indicates the age of the cluster — a lower turn-off point means the cluster is older [1].

practice_questions.text: Compare a Cepheid variable star and an eclipsing binary. In your answer, describe the physical cause of the brightness variation in each case and explain how each can be used to determine distance.
practice_questions.marks:
Cepheid variable:
• Brightness varies because the star physically pulsates (expands and contracts) [1]
• Period-luminosity relation: longer period = higher luminosity; measure period to find luminosity, compare with apparent magnitude to get distance [1]

Eclipsing binary:
• Brightness varies because one star passes in front of the other, blocking light (geometrical eclipse) [1]
• Can determine the orbital period and relative stellar sizes from the light curve; combined with spectral analysis gives true luminosities and hence distance [1]

practice_questions.text: Fatima Al-Rashid is an astronomy student at a sixth-form college in Sheffield. She observes a Cepheid variable in a distant galaxy. The star has a pulsation period of 10 days. Using the period-luminosity relation, she determines its absolute magnitude to be M = -3.0. She measures its apparent magnitude as m = +27.0. Calculate the distance to the galaxy in parsecs. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: m - M = 5 log10(d) - 5 [1]
Substitution: 27.0 - (-3.0) = 5 log10(d) - 5 → 30.0 = 5 log10(d) - 5 [1]
Rearrangement: log10(d) = (30.0 + 5) / 5 = 35 / 5 = 7.0 [1]
Answer: d = 10^7 = 10,000,000 parsecs (10 megaparsecs) [1]

practice_questions.text:
The Brackenfell Observing Society in Cumbria records a light curve for a variable star over several weeks. The light curve shows two dips per cycle: a deeper dip that reduces brightness by 40% and a shallower dip that reduces it by 15%, with a period between successive deep dips of 3.2 days.

Analyse what the light curve tells us about this star system. Include the likely type of variable star, the physical cause of each dip, what the dip depths indicate about the two stars, and what further observations would help characterise the system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Identifies eclipsing binary; explains both dips as geometric eclipses (one star crossing in front of the other); correctly interprets deeper dip as eclipse of the brighter star by the dimmer (more light blocked from total = dimmer star in front) or the brighter star being behind; shallower dip = dimmer star eclipsed; 3.2-day period is the orbital period; suggests spectroscopic radial velocity follow-up to get masses; suggests analysis of dip shapes to get stellar radii ratios; mentions the line-of-sight inclination requirement.

Secure (3-4): Correctly identifies eclipsing binary; explains eclipses cause dips; links depth to brightness ratio of the two stars; states orbital period; some mention of follow-up.

Developing (1-2): Correctly identifies variable star type or explains one dip; limited analysis.

Emerging (0): Irrelevant or no response.

knowledge_checks.q: Which region of the H-R diagram contains stars that are cool but very luminous?
What is the period-luminosity relation for Cepheid variables used for in astronomy?
options: Determining the distance to the Cepheid and its host galaxy
Detecting exoplanets in the habitable zone

knowledge_checks.q: The H-R diagram temperature axis has _____ temperature on the left and _____ temperature on the right.
An eclipsing binary light curve shows _____ brightness dips per orbital period, of different depths.
Match each type of star to its H-R diagram position.
right: Middle of the main sequence diagonal band

flashcard_questions.q: On the H-R diagram, which end of the x-axis is hot?
flashcard_questions.a: The left end (high temperature on the left, low temperature on the right).
A diagonal band on the H-R diagram where stars spend most of their lives fusing hydrogen in their cores.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do white dwarfs appear in the lower-left of the H-R diagram?
flashcard_questions.a: They are hot but very small, so their luminosity is low despite high surface temperature.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to a Sun-like star after it leaves the main sequence?
flashcard_questions.a: It expands into a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula, and leaves behind a white dwarf.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the main-sequence turn-off point of a star cluster tell us?
flashcard_questions.a: The cluster's age — older clusters have lower (dimmer) turn-off points.
Cepheid variables with longer pulsation periods have higher luminosities; used to find distances.

flashcard_questions.q: What causes the brightness variation in an eclipsing binary?
flashcard_questions.a: One star passes in front of the other, blocking some of its light as seen from Earth.
A sudden brightening caused by hydrogen accreted from a companion star igniting in a runaway fusion event on a white dwarf's surface.
A densely packed sphere of hundreds of thousands of old stars, found in a galaxy's halo.

flashcard_questions.q: How do high-mass stars end their lives differently from Sun-like stars?
flashcard_questions.a: High-mass stars explode as supernovae, leaving a neutron star or black hole; Sun-like stars form planetary nebulae and white dwarfs.
A shell of glowing gas expelled by a low-mass star at the end of its red giant phase, surrounding the white dwarf remnant.

glossary_terms.definition: A scatter plot of stellar luminosity against surface temperature, revealing distinct populations of stars at different evolutionary stages.
The diagonal band on the H-R diagram where stars fuse hydrogen in their cores; stars spend the majority of their lives here.
A shell of ionised gas ejected by a low-mass star at the end of its red giant phase, surrounding the hot white dwarf core.
A star whose observed brightness changes periodically, either due to physical pulsation or to another body eclipsing it.
A loose grouping of tens to hundreds of young stars formed from the same gas cloud, found in a galaxy's disc.
A densely packed, spherical collection of hundreds of thousands of old stars, found in a galaxy's halo.
A pulsating yellow supergiant whose period of variation is directly related to its luminosity, making it a standard candle for distance measurement.
